stem: Tariq, a 46-year-old bank manager with a BMI of 31 kg/m², attends a screening camp in Lahore. He has no symptoms. A random capillary glucose is 168 mg/dL. Which result would confirm a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?
options: A second random glucose of 170 mg/dL
A fasting plasma glucose of 112 mg/dL
explanation: In an asymptomatic person, diabetes is confirmed by two abnormal tests, such as HbA1c of 6.5 % or more on two occasions or fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or more. A fasting glucose of 112 mg/dL indicates impaired fasting glucose, and glycosuria is not diagnostic because renal thresholds vary.

stem: A 52-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. HbA1c is 7.6 %, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL (eGFR above 90), BMI 29 kg/m². She has no heart failure or cardiovascular disease. Diet advice has been given. Which drug is most appropriate to start?
explanation: Metformin is first-line for type 2 diabetes because it is effective, weight-neutral, does not cause hypoglycaemia on its own and is cheap. Glibenclamide causes hypoglycaemia and weight gain, and insulin is not first-line at this HbA1c without symptoms of severe hyperglycaemia.

stem: A 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes takes metformin 1 g twice daily. His creatinine has risen over a year and his eGFR is now 26 mL/min/1.73 m². He is clinically well. What is the most appropriate change to his metformin?
options: Reduce it to 500 mg twice daily
Switch to extended-release metformin at the same dose
explanation: Metformin should be stopped when eGFR falls below 30 because accumulation increases the risk of lactic acidosis; the dose is reduced when eGFR is between 30 and 45. Changing to extended-release metformin does not remove the risk of accumulation.

stem: A 74-year-old widow living alone in Gujranwala is brought in at 6 am sweating and confused. Capillary glucose is 38 mg/dL. She takes glibenclamide for diabetes and has been eating poorly with a cold. Creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL. Why is this drug a particular problem for her?
options: It causes lactic acidosis when the kidney function falls
It causes urinary loss of glucose and fluid
Its active metabolites accumulate in renal impairment
It increases insulin resistance in the liver
explanation: Glibenclamide is a long-acting sulfonylurea with active metabolites cleared by the kidney, so elderly people with reduced renal function and poor intake are at high risk of prolonged hypoglycaemia. Lactic acidosis is linked with metformin, and urinary glucose loss describes SGLT2 inhibitors.

stem: A 10-year-old girl from Abbottabad has had increased thirst, frequent urination and bedwetting for 3 weeks, with 3 kg weight loss. She is alert and well hydrated. Random glucose is 342 mg/dL; urine shows glucose 3+ and ketones 1+. Venous pH is 7.37. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Start metformin and review in a month
Dietary advice and repeat glucose in a week
Start subcutaneous insulin the same day
explanation: A thin child with osmotic symptoms, weight loss, hyperglycaemia and ketonuria has type 1 diabetes and needs insulin started the same day under a specialist team, to prevent progression to DKA. Oral agents have no role in type 1 diabetes.

stem: A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and had a myocardial infarction last year. HbA1c is 8.1 %, eGFR 58 mL/min/1.73 m². Which class of drug is most appropriate to add?
explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors such as empagliflozin or dapagliflozin lower glucose and reduce heart failure admissions, cardiovascular death and progression of kidney disease, so they are preferred in heart failure and atherosclerotic disease. Thiazolidinediones cause fluid retention and are contraindicated in heart failure.

stem: A 50-year-old woman has had type 2 diabetes for 7 years. Her blood pressure and creatinine are normal and urine dipstick shows no protein. Which test is most appropriate for annual screening for diabetic kidney disease?
explanation: Annual screening for diabetic kidney disease uses a spot urine albumin:creatinine ratio, which detects moderately increased albuminuria long before dipstick proteinuria, together with eGFR. A 24-hour collection is cumbersome and urea is an insensitive marker of kidney function.

stem: Sana, a 26-year-old with type 1 diabetes on basal-bolus insulin, has had vomiting and diarrhoea for a day and is eating very little, though she can keep fluids down. Her glucose is 250 mg/dL and blood ketones 0.8 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate advice about her insulin?
options: Stop all insulin until she is eating normally again
Stop the basal insulin and give rapid-acting insulin only with each meal
Continue basal insulin and check glucose and ketones every 2-4 hours
Halve all insulin doses and check her glucose once a day
explanation: During illness the stress response raises glucose even when little is eaten, so basal insulin must never be stopped in type 1 diabetes; glucose and ketones are checked every few hours and extra rapid-acting insulin is given if they rise. Stopping insulin is a classic precipitant of diabetic ketoacidosis. She needs urgent review if she cannot keep fluids down or her ketones keep rising.

stem: A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes for 15 years has his annual eye check. Fundoscopy shows fine new vessels on the optic disc and dot-blot haemorrhages in all quadrants. His vision is 6/9 in both eyes. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation: New vessels on the disc indicate proliferative diabetic retinopathy, which can bleed into the vitreous or cause tractional detachment, so urgent ophthalmology referral for panretinal photocoagulation (or anti-VEGF injection) is needed. Waiting 12 months risks sudden visual loss.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with long-standing diabetes and peripheral neuropathy has a hot, red, swollen right foot for 2 weeks after twisting it. The skin is intact with no ulcer, she has no fever, and pedal pulses are bounding. The foot is 3 °C warmer than the left. CRP is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Deep vein thrombosis of the calf
explanation: A warm, swollen, red foot with intact skin and good pulses in a person with neuropathy, often after minor trauma, is acute Charcot neuroarthropathy; it needs urgent offloading in a cast to prevent collapse of the midfoot. Cellulitis usually has a portal of entry, fever and raised inflammatory markers.

stem: At an annual diabetes review in a BHU, the medical officer wants to identify patients at risk of foot ulceration. Which bedside test best detects loss of protective sensation?
options: Joint position sense at the big toe
explanation: Inability to feel a 10 g monofilament at standard sites on the sole identifies loss of protective sensation and a high risk of ulceration. Ankle reflexes and joint position sense may be reduced in neuropathy but are not the standard screening tool.

stem: A 19-year-old man with type 1 diabetes has had vomiting and abdominal pain for a day after missing insulin. He is breathing deeply. Glucose 486 mg/dL, pH 7.12, bicarbonate 9 mmol/L, blood ketones 5.8 mmol/L, potassium 5.1 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Hyperglycaemia, acidosis (pH below 7.3, bicarbonate below 15) and raised ketones define diabetic ketoacidosis, here precipitated by missed insulin; deep Kussmaul breathing is respiratory compensation. HHS has marked hyperosmolality with little or no ketosis or acidosis.

stem: A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes arrives in the emergency department with DKA. Pulse 118/min, BP 96/60 mmHg. Glucose 520 mg/dL, pH 7.10, potassium 4.8 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate first step?
explanation: The first priority in DKA is restoring circulating volume with IV 0.9 % saline, followed by a fixed-rate IV insulin infusion and potassium replacement guided by levels. Bicarbonate is not routinely given and can worsen hypokalaemia and cerebral oedema.

stem: A 30-year-old man is being treated for DKA with IV fluids and a fixed-rate IV insulin infusion. After 6 hours his glucose has fallen to 230 mg/dL, but blood ketones are still 2.8 mmol/L and pH 7.24. What is the most appropriate change?
options: Stop the insulin infusion and start subcutaneous insulin
Add IV 10 % dextrose and continue the insulin infusion
explanation: Ketosis and acidosis have not resolved, so insulin must continue to switch off ketogenesis; dextrose is added when glucose falls below about 250 mg/dL (14 mmol/L) to prevent hypoglycaemia. Stopping or reducing the insulin because glucose has fallen is a common error that prolongs DKA.

stem: An 8-year-old boy is 5 hours into treatment for severe DKA. He now complains of headache, becomes irritable, and his pulse falls from 120 to 64/min with a rise in blood pressure. Glucose is 260 mg/dL. What is the most likely complication?
explanation: Headache, irritability, falling heart rate and rising blood pressure during DKA treatment in a child suggest cerebral oedema, the main cause of death in paediatric DKA; it is treated urgently with mannitol or hypertonic saline. The glucose is not low, and hypokalaemia causes arrhythmia and weakness rather than these signs.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is brought from her home in Sukkur during a heatwave. She has been drowsy for 3 days with poor fluid intake. Glucose 920 mg/dL, sodium 148 mmol/L, urea high, serum osmolality 356 mOsm/kg, pH 7.36, blood ketones 0.6 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Very high glucose, osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg and marked dehydration without significant acidosis or ketosis define hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state, typical in elderly people with type 2 diabetes. In DKA the pH would be below 7.3 with ketones above 3 mmol/L.

stem: A 36-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is brought to the emergency department unconscious after a long football match. Capillary glucose is 32 mg/dL. He has a working intravenous cannula. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Oral glucose gel between the gums
explanation: Severe hypoglycaemia in an unconscious patient with IV access is treated with IV glucose (for example 10 % glucose), then a long-acting carbohydrate once awake. Oral glucose is unsafe when consciousness is impaired; IM glucagon is the alternative when there is no IV access.

stem: A 45-year-old woman on insulin feels shaky and sweaty at work. She is fully alert and able to swallow. Capillary glucose is 58 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate first treatment?
options: 15 to 20 g of glucose tablets or juice
A full meal of rice and curry
A chocolate bar and recheck glucose in an hour
explanation: Conscious hypoglycaemia is treated with 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate (glucose tablets, juice), rechecking after 10 to 15 minutes and following with a longer-acting snack. Chocolate and full meals contain fat that slows glucose absorption, and glucagon is for patients who cannot take oral treatment.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has palpitations, heat intolerance and weight loss. She has a diffuse smooth goitre with a bruit, proptosis and lid lag. TSH is undetectable and free T4 is raised. Which test best confirms the cause?
explanation: A diffuse goitre with bruit and eye signs in a hyperthyroid young woman is Graves disease, confirmed by TSH receptor (stimulating) antibodies. Anti-TPO antibodies are found in Graves but are much more typical of Hashimoto thyroiditis and are not specific.

stem: Sana, 32, was started on carbimazole for Graves disease 5 weeks ago. She now has a sore throat and fever of 38.6 °C. She has no cough. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: Start oral amoxicillin and continue the carbimazole
Throat swab and review in 3 days
Stop carbimazole and check a full blood count
explanation: Sore throat or fever on an antithyroid drug may signal agranulocytosis, so the drug is stopped and an urgent full blood count checked. Propylthiouracil can also cause agranulocytosis, so switching to it is unsafe.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has had a painful, tender swelling in the front of her neck, fever and palpitations for 10 days, beginning two weeks after a sore throat. ESR is 78 mm/h, free T4 is raised and TSH is suppressed. A technetium scan shows very low thyroid uptake. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A painful, tender thyroid after a viral illness, with a high ESR, thyrotoxicosis and low isotope uptake, is subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis: hormone leaks from damaged follicles rather than being overproduced. It is treated with NSAIDs and a beta-blocker, not antithyroid drugs. Graves disease is painless and shows diffusely increased uptake.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with untreated Graves disease is admitted after a cholecystectomy with temperature 40.1 °C, agitation, vomiting and atrial fibrillation at 164/min. Propranolol is started. Which additional drug most directly blocks both new hormone synthesis and peripheral conversion of T4 to T3?
explanation: In thyroid storm, propylthiouracil is preferred because it blocks thyroid hormone synthesis and also inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to T3; iodide is given at least an hour later to block release. Carbimazole blocks synthesis only, and iodide given first could fuel further hormone production.

stem: A 34-year-old woman had a sore throat 2 weeks ago. She now has fever, neck pain radiating to the jaw, palpitations and a very tender thyroid. ESR is 92 mm/h, TSH is suppressed and free T4 high. Technetium scan shows almost no uptake. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Painful thyroid, high ESR, thyrotoxicosis and low uptake after a viral illness indicate subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis; the thyrotoxicosis comes from release of stored hormone, so NSAIDs (or steroids if severe) and beta-blockers are used. Antithyroid drugs do not help because new hormone synthesis is not increased.

stem: A 44-year-old woman has tiredness, weight gain, constipation and heavy periods. She has a firm, non-tender diffuse goitre. TSH is 38 mU/L (normal 0.4-4.0) and free T4 is low. Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies are strongly positive. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Hypothyroidism with a firm goitre and positive anti-TPO antibodies is Hashimoto thyroiditis, treated with lifelong levothyroxine titrated to TSH. Iodide does not treat autoimmune hypothyroidism and can worsen it, and liothyronine is not used as standard replacement.

stem: A 76-year-old man with stable angina is found to have primary hypothyroidism. TSH is 24 mU/L and free T4 is low. What is the most appropriate way to start treatment?
options: Full replacement dose of levothyroxine from the first day
Delay treatment until his angina is revascularised
explanation: In elderly patients and those with ischaemic heart disease, levothyroxine is started at a low dose (such as 25 micrograms daily) and increased gradually, because a rapid rise in metabolic rate can provoke angina or arrhythmia. A full dose from the start is appropriate only for younger, fit patients.

stem: A 39-year-old woman had thyroid tests during a health check. She has no symptoms and is not pregnant or planning pregnancy. TSH is 7.2 mU/L (normal 0.4-4.0) and free T4 is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat TSH and free T4 in about 3 months
explanation: A mildly raised TSH with normal free T4 is subclinical hypothyroidism; a single result may be transient, so tests are repeated in about 3 months (often with anti-TPO antibodies) before deciding on treatment. Levothyroxine is usually considered for persistent TSH above 10 or in pregnancy, and ultrasound is not needed without a palpable abnormality.

stem: A 37-year-old woman has a 2 cm painless lump in the right lobe of the thyroid. TSH is normal. Ultrasound shows a solid hypoechoic nodule with microcalcifications and irregular margins. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation: A euthyroid nodule with suspicious ultrasound features (hypoechoic, microcalcification, irregular margins) needs fine-needle aspiration cytology. Isotope scanning is used when TSH is low to look for a hot nodule, and thyroglobulin is used for follow-up after cancer treatment, not diagnosis.

stem: A 29-year-old woman from Karachi has a slowly growing thyroid nodule and a firm 1.5 cm lymph node in the same side of the neck. She is euthyroid. Fine-needle aspiration shows cells with nuclear grooves, pale 'Orphan Annie' nuclei and intranuclear inclusions. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Nuclear grooves, clear nuclei and intranuclear inclusions are characteristic of papillary carcinoma, the most common thyroid cancer, which typically spreads to cervical lymph nodes in young women. Follicular carcinoma cannot be diagnosed on cytology because it requires capsular or vascular invasion on histology and spreads by blood.

stem: A 35-year-old man with Graves disease has gritty eyes, mild proptosis and periorbital swelling. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and is controlled on carbimazole. He asks what he can do to protect his eyes. Which measure most reduces the risk of his eye disease worsening?
explanation: Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for developing and worsening thyroid eye disease, and stopping smoking improves outcome and response to treatment. Tinted glasses help symptoms of photophobia but do not change the course of the disease, and switching antithyroid drugs has no effect on the eyes.

stem: A 66-year-old man has taken amiodarone for 18 months for recurrent ventricular tachycardia. He now has fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation. TSH is 19 mU/L and free T4 is low. His cardiologist says amiodarone is essential. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Stop amiodarone and recheck thyroid tests in 3 months
explanation: Amiodarone's high iodine content can cause hypothyroidism through the Wolff-Chaikoff effect, especially in people with underlying autoimmune thyroiditis; it is treated with levothyroxine while continuing amiodarone if it is needed. Carbimazole and perchlorate are used for amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis, not hypothyroidism.

stem: A 33-year-old woman has 4 months of fatigue, weight loss, dizziness on standing and darkening of her palmar creases and gums. BP is 92/60 mmHg lying and 78/50 mmHg standing. Sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L. Which test best confirms the likely diagnosis?
explanation: Hyperpigmentation, postural hypotension, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia suggest primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), confirmed by a failure of cortisol to rise after synthetic ACTH in a short Synacthen test. The dexamethasone suppression test is used to screen for cortisol excess, the opposite problem.

stem: A 41-year-old man with known Addison disease is brought in after 2 days of vomiting and diarrhoea, unable to keep down his tablets. He is drowsy; BP 78/44 mmHg, glucose 62 mg/dL, sodium 124 mmol/L. What is the most important immediate treatment?
options: Intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg after a Synacthen test
explanation: Adrenal crisis is treated immediately with IV (or IM) hydrocortisone 100 mg, IV 0.9 % saline and glucose as needed. Oral treatment cannot be absorbed with vomiting, and delaying steroid for a Synacthen test is unnecessary in a known patient and dangerous.

stem: A 47-year-old man from a village in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has Addison disease confirmed by a short Synacthen test. He was treated for pulmonary TB 15 years ago. CT shows small, bilaterally calcified adrenal glands. What is the most likely cause of his adrenal failure?
explanation: Bilateral adrenal calcification with a history of TB points to tuberculous adrenalitis, still an important cause of Addison disease in countries with high TB burden. Autoimmune adrenalitis is the commonest cause worldwide, but it produces small adrenals without calcification.

stem: A 63-year-old man who smokes 40 cigarettes a day has 6 weeks of rapidly worsening weakness, ankle swelling and weight loss. BP 168/98 mmHg. Potassium 2.6 mmol/L, bicarbonate 34 mmol/L, glucose 240 mg/dL. Cortisol is high and ACTH markedly raised. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Cushing disease from an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma
Ectopic ACTH secretion from small cell lung cancer
explanation: Rapid onset of hypokalaemic alkalosis, weakness, hyperglycaemia and very high ACTH in a heavy smoker suggests ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer; there is often little time for classic Cushingoid features to develop. An adrenal adenoma would suppress ACTH, and pituitary Cushing disease usually gives only moderately raised ACTH and a slower course.

stem: A 38-year-old woman has central obesity, purple abdominal striae, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness and new hypertension. She takes no steroid medicines, creams or injections. Which is the most appropriate first-line screening test?
explanation: Suspected Cushing syndrome is screened with the overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test (or late-night salivary cortisol or 24-hour urinary free cortisol); failure to suppress cortisol suggests excess. A random cortisol is unhelpful because of diurnal variation, and ACTH and imaging are used only after cortisol excess is confirmed.

stem: A 52-year-old woman from rural Punjab has a round face, central obesity, thin skin and bruises. For a year she has taken powders from a local hakeem for joint pain. 9 am cortisol is low and ACTH is low. What is the most likely cause of her features?
explanation: Cushingoid features with suppressed cortisol and ACTH mean the glucocorticoid is coming from outside; unlabelled remedies containing steroids are a well-known cause in Pakistan. She is at risk of adrenal crisis if the remedy is stopped suddenly. An adrenal carcinoma would give high cortisol with low ACTH.

stem: A 39-year-old man has hypertension of 168/102 mmHg despite amlodipine and ramipril. Potassium is 2.9 mmol/L without diuretics or vomiting. Sodium is 143 mmol/L. Which is the most appropriate initial investigation for the likely cause?
explanation: Resistant hypertension with spontaneous hypokalaemia suggests primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome), screened with the aldosterone:renin ratio. ACE inhibitors raise renin and can give false negatives, so results are interpreted with this in mind; metanephrines are for phaeochromocytoma, which causes paroxysmal symptoms.

stem: A 34-year-old woman has episodes of pounding headache, palpitations, sweating and pallor. BP between attacks is 162/104 mmHg. Plasma free metanephrines are markedly raised and CT shows a 4 cm right adrenal mass. Surgery is planned. Which drug should be started first?
explanation: Phaeochromocytoma needs alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) for 1 to 2 weeks before surgery, with a beta-blocker added only after alpha-blockade if tachycardia persists. Starting a beta-blocker first leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can cause a hypertensive crisis.

stem: A 44-year-old man from Faisalabad notices that his rings and shoes no longer fit. He has coarse facial features, a large tongue, sweaty doughy hands and recently diagnosed hypertension. What is the most appropriate initial blood test?
explanation: Enlarging hands and feet with coarse features suggest acromegaly, and serum IGF-1 is the best screening test because it reflects average growth hormone secretion over the day. A random growth hormone level is unreliable because secretion is pulsatile; failure of growth hormone to suppress during an oral glucose tolerance test confirms the diagnosis.

stem: A 45-year-old man notices his rings and shoes no longer fit. He has coarse facial features, a protruding jaw, sweating, carpal tunnel syndrome and new hypertension. Which test best confirms the likely diagnosis?
options: Growth hormone after a 75 g oral glucose load
explanation: Acromegaly is confirmed by failure of growth hormone to suppress after a 75 g oral glucose load, usually with a raised IGF-1. A random GH is unreliable because secretion is pulsatile, and prolactin may be raised but does not confirm GH excess.

stem: A 50-year-old man keeps bumping into door frames on both sides. MRI shows a large pituitary macroadenoma extending upwards. Which visual field defect is most likely?
explanation: A pituitary tumour growing upwards compresses the optic chiasm from below, damaging the crossing nasal fibres and causing bitemporal hemianopia, often starting in the upper quadrants. Homonymous hemianopia arises from lesions behind the chiasm, such as in the optic tract or occipital cortex.

stem: Parveen, 30, delivered at home in rural Balochistan 6 months ago and had a severe postpartum haemorrhage needing transfusion. She could not breastfeed, has had no periods since, and feels tired and cold. BP 96/60 mmHg, sodium 129 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Massive postpartum haemorrhage can cause ischaemic necrosis of the enlarged pituitary (Sheehan syndrome), shown by failure of lactation, amenorrhoea and features of secondary hypothyroidism and cortisol deficiency. Asherman syndrome causes amenorrhoea from uterine scarring but does not affect lactation or cause hypotension and hyponatraemia.

stem: A 66-year-old smoker with a newly found lung mass is mildly confused. He is clinically euvolaemic. Sodium 122 mmol/L, serum osmolality 254 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 520 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 48 mmol/L. TSH and cortisol are normal. He has no seizures. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine and high urine sodium, with normal thyroid and adrenal function, is SIADH, here likely from small cell lung cancer; first-line treatment of mild symptoms is fluid restriction. Normal saline can worsen hyponatraemia in SIADH, and hypertonic saline is for severe symptoms such as seizures.

stem: A 44-year-old woman on long-term lithium for bipolar disorder passes 6 litres of dilute urine a day. Glucose and calcium are normal. During a water deprivation test her urine osmolality stays low, and after desmopressin it rises by less than 10 %. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Failure to concentrate urine with water deprivation and no response to desmopressin indicates nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, a recognised effect of lithium on the collecting ducts. In cranial DI the urine concentrates well after desmopressin, and in primary polydipsia it concentrates with water deprivation alone.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has a corrected calcium of 11.6 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.2) found on routine tests, with low phosphate. Parathyroid hormone is raised. She had a renal stone last year. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: High calcium with an inappropriately raised PTH and low phosphate is primary hyperparathyroidism, usually from a single parathyroid adenoma; renal stones are a classic complication. In malignancy and vitamin D toxicity PTH is suppressed, and secondary hyperparathyroidism has a low or normal calcium.

stem: A 62-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is drowsy, thirsty and constipated. Corrected calcium is 14.2 mg/dL, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, PTH suppressed. She is clinically dehydrated. What is the most appropriate first treatment?
explanation: Severe hypercalcaemia causes dehydration through nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, so the first step is IV saline rehydration, followed by an IV bisphosphonate. Loop diuretics are no longer used routinely and can worsen dehydration, and steroids help mainly in lymphoma or vitamin D-mediated hypercalcaemia.

stem: A 54-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease has bone pain and itching. Which pattern of results is most likely?
options: Calcium high, phosphate low, PTH high
Calcium low, phosphate high, PTH high
Calcium high, phosphate high, PTH low
Calcium normal, phosphate low, PTH low
explanation: In CKD, phosphate retention and reduced renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation of vitamin D lower calcium, which drives secondary hyperparathyroidism with high PTH. High calcium with low phosphate and high PTH is the pattern of primary hyperparathyroidism.

stem: Nusrat, a 34-year-old mother of four who keeps purdah and rarely goes outdoors, has aching bones, a waddling gait and difficulty climbing stairs. Calcium is low, phosphate low, alkaline phosphatase raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Osteomalacia due to vitamin D deficiency
explanation: Bone pain, proximal myopathy and low calcium and phosphate with raised ALP are typical of osteomalacia, common in Pakistani women with little sun exposure and repeated pregnancies. Osteoporosis causes no symptoms until fracture and has normal biochemistry.

stem: A 40-year-old woman had a total thyroidectomy for a large goitre yesterday. She now has tingling of the fingers and lips and painful spasms of the hands. Corrected calcium is 6.6 mg/dL. ECG shows a prolonged QT interval. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
explanation: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia with tetany and QT prolongation after thyroidectomy, from damage to the parathyroids, needs slow IV calcium gluconate, followed by oral calcium and active vitamin D. Oral treatment alone is too slow for symptomatic severe hypocalcaemia.

stem: A 36-year-old man has recurrent renal stones with raised calcium and PTH. He also has galactorrhoea with a raised prolactin and has had several peptic ulcers with a high fasting gastrin. His father had a 'gland operation in the neck'. Which condition is most likely?
explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism with a pituitary tumour (here a prolactinoma) and a pancreatic or duodenal tumour (gastrinoma) is MEN1, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. MEN2A combines medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism, without pituitary or gastrinoma tumours.

stem: A 38-year-old slim man was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 9 months ago and started on metformin, then gliclazide. Despite good adherence, his HbA1c has risen from 7.4 % to 10.2 % and he has lost weight. GAD antibodies are strongly positive and C-peptide is low. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Rapid failure of oral agents in a slim adult with positive GAD antibodies and low C-peptide indicates latent autoimmune diabetes in adults, a slowly progressive form of type 1 diabetes that needs insulin. Further oral agents depend on beta-cell function that is being lost.

stem: A 47-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes for 25 years has early fullness, bloating and vomiting of food eaten many hours earlier. Her glucose readings have become erratic, with unexpected lows after meals. Endoscopy shows food residue but no obstruction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Autonomic neuropathy in long-standing diabetes delays gastric emptying, causing early satiety, vomiting of old food and mismatched insulin timing with post-meal hypoglycaemia. Endoscopy excluding obstruction makes pyloric stricture and malignancy unlikely; a gastric emptying study confirms the diagnosis.

stem: Kiran, 31, received 4 units of red cells for a postpartum haemorrhage 5 weeks ago. She had gestational diabetes and her home fasting glucose readings are now 130 to 150 mg/dL. Her HbA1c is 5.3 %. What is the best explanation for this discrepancy?
options: Home glucose meters read falsely high after delivery
Gestational diabetes has fully resolved since the delivery
HbA1c is falsely high after transfusion
Young and transfused red cells are less glycated
explanation: HbA1c reflects glycation of haemoglobin over the lifespan of red cells; after blood loss and transfusion, the circulating cells are younger or donor-derived, so HbA1c is falsely low. Glucose readings or an oral glucose tolerance test should be used to assess her glycaemia instead.

stem: A 22-year-old man with DKA has a serum potassium of 5.2 mmol/L on arrival. The registrar plans to add potassium chloride to the IV fluids once insulin is running and potassium falls below 5.5 mmol/L. Why is this necessary?
options: Saline infusion causes renal potassium retention
Acidosis worsens as the serum potassium falls further
Ketones bind potassium in the blood
explanation: In DKA total body potassium is depleted through osmotic diuresis and vomiting, but acidosis and insulin deficiency shift potassium out of cells so the serum level looks normal or high. Insulin moves potassium back into cells, so serum potassium falls quickly and replacement is needed to avoid dangerous hypokalaemia.

stem: A 71-year-old woman has palpitations and weight loss. She has had a lumpy goitre for many years. TSH is suppressed and free T3 high. TSH receptor antibodies are negative. Technetium scan shows several areas of increased uptake with suppression of the rest of the gland. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Patchy uptake in several autonomous nodules with suppression of the rest of the gland in an older woman with a long-standing nodular goitre is toxic multinodular goitre. Graves disease shows diffuse uniform uptake with positive TSH receptor antibodies, and subacute thyroiditis shows low uptake.

stem: A 42-year-old man has a hard thyroid nodule. His brother had an adrenal tumour removed after attacks of high blood pressure. Histology after thyroidectomy shows nests of cells in an amyloid-containing stroma. Which serum marker is most useful for follow-up?
explanation: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, shows amyloid stroma and secretes calcitonin (and CEA), which is used to monitor for recurrence; the family history suggests MEN2. Thyroglobulin is the follow-up marker for papillary and follicular cancers, which arise from follicular cells.

stem: A 78-year-old woman is found drowsy at home in winter. Temperature 33.8 °C, pulse 46/min, BP 94/58 mmHg. She has periorbital puffiness and slow-relaxing reflexes. Sodium 122 mmol/L, glucose 64 mg/dL. TSH is very high. Adrenal function has not been tested. Which drug should be given together with thyroid hormone replacement?
explanation: Myxoedema coma is treated with IV thyroid hormone plus IV hydrocortisone, because coexisting adrenal insufficiency is possible and thyroid hormone increases cortisol clearance, which can precipitate adrenal crisis. Supportive warming, glucose and ventilation as needed are also given.

stem: A 36-year-old teacher with Addison disease takes hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. She now has influenza with fever of 38.6 °C but is eating and drinking normally. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Stop fludrocortisone until she is well
Double the hydrocortisone dose during the fever
Switch to intravenous hydrocortisone given at home by a relative
explanation: Sick day rules for adrenal insufficiency are to double the oral glucocorticoid dose during fever or significant illness, and to use injectable hydrocortisone and seek help if vomiting. Continuing the usual dose risks adrenal crisis because cortisol needs rise with illness.

stem: A 56-year-old man with a known non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma develops a sudden severe headache, vomiting and double vision. He has a third nerve palsy and BP 86/52 mmHg. CT shows haemorrhage within an enlarged pituitary. What is the most urgent treatment?
explanation: Pituitary apoplexy is haemorrhage or infarction of a pituitary tumour; acute ACTH deficiency causes life-threatening adrenal insufficiency, so IV hydrocortisone is given urgently, with neurosurgical review for decompression. Lumbar puncture is not needed once imaging shows the cause and is risky with raised pressure.

stem: A 45-year-old woman recovering from removal of a pituitary macroadenoma has low free T4 with a low TSH, and low 9 am cortisol. She is clinically stable. What is the most appropriate order of hormone replacement?
options: Levothyroxine first, then hydrocortisone after a week
Levothyroxine only, as cortisol will recover
explanation: Glucocorticoid replacement must begin before thyroxine, because thyroxine speeds cortisol metabolism and can precipitate adrenal crisis in untreated ACTH deficiency. Mineralocorticoid is usually not needed in pituitary disease because the renin-angiotensin system still drives aldosterone.

stem: A 2-year-old boy from a poor area of Karachi was exclusively breastfed until 18 months and rarely goes outside. He has bowed legs, swollen wrists and a row of bumps along the costochondral junctions. ALP is raised and phosphate low. Which X-ray finding at the wrist is most expected?
options: Cupping and fraying of the metaphyses
Periosteal new bone with subperiosteal haemorrhage
explanation: Nutritional rickets from vitamin D deficiency causes widened, cupped and frayed metaphyses at the wrist, matching the clinical wrist widening and rachitic rosary. Subperiosteal haemorrhage suggests scurvy, and dense metaphyseal bands are seen in lead poisoning.

stem: A 32-year-old man has a corrected calcium of 10.9 mg/dL and a PTH at the upper limit of normal. He has no symptoms, no stones and normal bone density. His mother and uncle had 'high calcium' that was never treated. Which test best distinguishes the likely diagnosis from primary hyperparathyroidism?
explanation: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, an autosomal dominant defect of the calcium-sensing receptor, gives mild lifelong hypercalcaemia with very low urinary calcium excretion (clearance ratio below 0.01); it needs no surgery. A sestamibi scan localises an adenoma but cannot separate the two conditions.

stem: A 14-year-old girl is short with a round face and short fourth and fifth metacarpals. She has had cramps and tingling. Calcium is low, phosphate high and PTH markedly raised. Magnesium and vitamin D are normal, and kidney function is normal. What is the underlying problem?
explanation: Low calcium and high phosphate despite a high PTH with normal kidneys mean the tissues are not responding to PTH (pseudohypoparathyroidism); the body habitus is Albright hereditary osteodystrophy. In true hypoparathyroidism PTH would be low.

stem: A medical officer at a BHU in a remote valley of Gilgit-Baltistan notices that many women and schoolchildren have diffuse, painless goitres. Most are clinically euthyroid. Which public health measure is most appropriate?
options: Referral of all goitres for thyroidectomy
explanation: Endemic diffuse goitre in mountainous areas of northern Pakistan is due to iodine deficiency, best prevented by universal salt iodisation. Levothyroxine for everyone and routine surgery treat individuals but do not address the cause, and mass ultrasound adds cost without benefit.

stem: A 57-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is admitted 2 days after a hernia repair with vomiting and rapid breathing. Glucose 196 mg/dL, pH 7.14, bicarbonate 10 mmol/L, blood ketones 5.6 mmol/L. His diabetes medicines were continued around surgery. Which drug most likely contributed?
explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin can cause euglycaemic DKA, with ketoacidosis at only modestly raised glucose, especially around surgery, fasting or acute illness; they are usually withheld before operations. Metformin is associated with lactic acidosis, not ketoacidosis.
